
### address format {.smaller}

*  RFC 5322
<hr/>
*  `Name For Humans <username@dns.name.example>`
*  `username@dns.name.example`
   *  this part called "addr-spec"
*  destination is from _MX record_ for dns.name.example
<hr/>
*  `username@[machine.dns.name.example]`
*  `username@[203.0.113.5]`
*  destination is machine.dns.name.exmaple/203.0.113.5

### MX records {.smaller}

```
gmail.com.              639     IN      MX      5 gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
gmail.com.              639     IN      MX      10 alt1.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
gmail.com.              639     IN      MX      20 alt2.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
gmail.com.              639     IN      MX      30 alt3.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
gmail.com.              639     IN      MX      40 alt4.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.
```
<hr/>
*  5/10/20/... is preference (lower = more preferred) 
*  client should try servers in order
   *  lookup A or AAAA record for each
   *  use first that works
*  if no MX record, fallback to looking up address for name

### layers of forwarding

*  emails to <i>xyz</i>@virginia.edu would go to mailbox on...
   *  Microsoft-hosted email servers
   *  Google-hosted email servers (during transition)
   *  ticketing systems (cshelpdesk@virginia.edu, ...)
   *  mailing list systems (csugrads@virginia.edu, ...)
   *  ...
*  likely all hosted on different servers
*  MX record will only have one of those...

### email relays

*  many mail servers are relays
   *  collect message, send on to actual destination
*  "submission servers" --- special case of relays
   *  mail user agent sends message to one submission server, then forgets about it
   *  simplifies logic of mail user agents
   *  submission server can handle retrying, etc.
